: Data sources available via `download_data()` in [tidyfinance]{.pkg}. For every dataset with a time dimension, the same `start_date` and `end_date` arguments subset the returned panel to a user-specified window. {#tbl-data-sources}
```{=latex}
\endgroup
```

Most rows in @tbl-data-sources mirror upstream providers; the high-frequency dataset is the exception. We host it ourselves: it comprises message-level snapshots of the NASDAQ limit order book for the SPY exchange-traded fund (and TLT for government bonds) from July 2007 to October 2025, more than 30 billion order-book messages in total, curated for the analysis in @menkveld.2026.

A first illustration uses only public data sources. We retrieve the current constituents of the Dow Jones Industrial Average and then download daily prices for those tickers over a chosen window. `list_supported_indexes()` returns the full set of equity indexes available through the `"constituents"` domain.

```{r}
#| label: example-dow-constituents
#| message: false
dow_constituents <- download_data(
  domain = "constituents",
  index = "Dow Jones Industrial Average"
)
download_data(
  domain = "stock_prices",
  symbols = dow_constituents$symbol,
  start_date = "2020-01-01",
  end_date = "2024-12-31"
)
```

Similarly, we can fetch the Fama-French three-factor data from Ken French's Data Library with a single call to download and parse the published archives):
```{r}
#| label: example-ff-factors
ff_factors <- download_data(
  domain = "factors_ff",
  dataset = "Fama/French 3 Factors",
  start_date = "1972-01-01",
  end_date = "2024-12-31"
)
```

The `start_date` and `end_date` arguments generalize across every dataset type in @tbl-data-sources that supports a time dimension.

Public data still need nontrivial cleaning. The Goyal-Welch [@goyal.2008] macroeconomic predictors are a typical case: `download_data(domain = "macro_predictors", dataset = "monthly")` fetches the raw spreadsheet at the requested frequency (set `dataset` to `monthly`, `quarterly`, or `annual`), parses dates from the native `yyyymm`, `yyyyq`, or `yyyy` format, strips comma thousand separators, and coerces character columns to numeric. It then constructs the standard predictors used in the equity-premium prediction literature: the log dividend-price ratio (`dp`), dividend yield (`dy`), earnings-price ratio (`ep`), dividend-payout ratio (`de`), the forward equity risk premium (`rp_div`), the term spread (`tms`), and the default-yield spread (`dfy`). The output is the cleaned panel filtered to the requested date range.

For empirical asset pricing work, WRDS is the gold-standard source of return and accounting panels. WRDS data are proprietary, so an institutional subscription and credentials are required. [tidyfinance]{.pkg} handles this once. `set_wrds_credentials()` prompts for the username and password and stores them in a project-specific or global `.Renviron` file, and prompts the user to add `.Renviron` to `.gitignore` to prevent credential leakage. Subsequent `download_data()` calls open the database connection automatically. Depending on the user's WRDS account settings, `download_data()` may also trigger a two-factor authentication (2FA) challenge that WRDS sends to the registered device; once approved, the connection proceeds normally.

`download_data()` applies standard cleaning conventions following @bali.2016 and @scheuch.2023 automatically. For CRSP monthly data, the function restricts the universe to common equity securities listed on NYSE, AMEX (now NYSE American), or NASDAQ. It computes market capitalization as shares outstanding times price, constructs a one-month market capitalization lag for portfolio weights, and maps listing exchange codes and Standard Industrial Classification (SIC) codes to readable labels. Excess returns are raw returns minus a risk-free rate that [tidyfinance]{.pkg} constructs from FRED by splicing the 3-month Treasury bill secondary-market rate (pre-2001) with the 4-week Treasury bill secondary-market rate (from 2001 onward); the spliced series is hosted on Hugging Face and refreshed monthly by a scheduled GitHub Actions workflow. Observations with missing returns or market capitalization are dropped. Delisting returns are incorporated directly, eliminating the need for a separate adjustment. The function defaults to the CRSP 2.0 layout introduced in February 2024; passing `version = "v1"` returns the legacy layout for replication of studies built on the earlier release.

For Compustat annual data, `download_data()` restricts to industrial-format consolidated statements and retains only the most recent observation per firm-year. It constructs book equity in priority order: stockholders' equity when available, else common equity plus preferred stock, else total assets minus total liabilities. The function adds back deferred taxes and investment tax credits, and subtracts the book value of preferred stock.

For TRACE corporate bond transactions, `download_data()` applies the Dick-Nielsen cleaning protocol [@dicknielsen.2009] to remove cancellations, corrections, and reversals before returning the trade panel.

Across `download_data()`, every returned panel exposes a single `date` column of `<date>` type, regardless of source. Joining observations from different providers therefore reduces to an equality join on `date` without manual format conversion. The convention is the same across frequencies: daily observations return the trading date, monthly observations the last calendar day of the reference month (regardless of whether it was a trading day), and quarterly and annual observations the fiscal period-end date as reported by the original source. For Compustat, the latter is the firm's fiscal year-end (`datadate`), which is typically December of the fiscal year but can differ across firms and within firms across years. Macroeconomic series from FRED keep their original release dates. Where the underlying source uses an internal date that differs from this convention, [tidyfinance]{.pkg} preserves it as an auxiliary column: CRSP 2.0 monthly returns, for example, retain the trading-date `mthcaldt` as `calculation_date` alongside the harmonized `date`. Cross-frequency joins, such as merging monthly returns with annual fundamentals, require the lagging logic described in @sec-variable-construction.

### Variable construction {#sec-variable-construction}

Most predictive variables in asset pricing studies are based on lagged information so that, for example, portfolio formation in month $t$ always uses only data observable at the end of month $t-1$. `add_lagged_columns()` automates the required lagging procedure. For each row in the data, it looks back over a configurable window and attaches the most recent observed value of the chosen columns. @fig-lagging-illustration illustrates the two modes the function supports. By default (`ff_adjustment = FALSE`), shown in Panel A, the window is bounded by `lag` (the minimum delay between observation and use) and `max_lag` (the maximum delay before a stale value is treated as missing). Within this window (the dashed rectangle), the function picks the most recent non-missing value; if no observation falls in the window, the lagged column takes `NA`.

The second mode, enabled by `ff_adjustment = TRUE` and shown in Panel B of @fig-lagging-illustration, implements the Fama-French convention [@fama.1993]. Accounting variables for fiscal year $t-1$ are assumed to become public information by June of year $t$ and are then used for portfolio formation from July of $t$ through June of $t+1$. This produces a step-function lag that updates once per year at the June/July boundary, regardless of the underlying fiscal year-end: all months from July through June share the value locked in at the previous rebalancing.

`join_lagged_values()` is a related helper that merges lagged values from one data frame into another using the same windowing logic. It is useful when the target panel and the source panel are at different frequencies, for example when joining monthly accounting data into a quarterly target panel. The function takes the same `ff_adjustment` argument as `add_lagged_columns()`, so the Fama-French convention can be applied at the join step rather than as a separate transformation.

```{r}
#| label: fig-lagging-illustration
#| fig-cap: "Two lagging mechanisms in `add_lagged_columns()`. Each row represents a data series with observed (filled) and missing (hollow) cells. The dashed rectangle marks the search window from the perspective of the most recent observation (the top row); arrows show which value gets matched to each target month. Panel A (`ff_adjustment = FALSE`) returns the most recent observed value within a window bounded by `lag` and `max_lag`. Panel B (`ff_adjustment = TRUE`) implements the Fama-French convention, where the lagged value updates only at the June/July boundary and is held constant for the next twelve months."
#| fig-width: 6.5
#| fig-height: 4
#| out-width: "100%"
#| fig-pos: "H"
#| echo: false
ts <- 0.94
corner <- unit(4, "pt")


# Extra padding so the dashed box extends slightly beyond the tiles
win_pad <- 0.15

# Extend data back by one month (Nov Y-2) so Year T-2 has a real bracket span
month_labels <- month.abb[c(11, 12, 1:12, 1:7)]
n <- length(month_labels)

x_labels <- -0.8
x_ff <- 0.55
x_std <- 3.0

obs_pattern <- c(
  FALSE, #  1  Nov Y-2
  TRUE, #  2  Dec Y-2  (fiscal year-end Y-2)
  FALSE, #  3  Jan Y-1
  FALSE, #  4  Feb Y-1
  FALSE, #  5  Mar Y-1
  FALSE, #  6  Apr Y-1
  TRUE, #  7  May Y-1
  FALSE, #  8  Jun Y-1
  FALSE, #  9  Jul Y-1
  TRUE, # 10  Aug Y-1
  FALSE, # 11  Sep Y-1
  TRUE, # 12  Oct Y-1
  FALSE, # 13  Nov Y-1
  TRUE, # 14  Dec Y-1  (fiscal year-end Y-1)
  TRUE, # 15  Jan Y
  FALSE, # 16  Feb Y
  TRUE, # 17  Mar Y
  FALSE, # 18  Apr Y
  TRUE, # 19  May Y
  FALSE, # 20  Jun Y
  TRUE # 21  Jul Y
)

df_data <- data.frame(
  y = 1:n,
  label = month_labels,
  observed = obs_pattern,
  # Data recency: older months fade toward transparent, newer ones solid
  alpha = 0.35 + 0.65 * ((1:n) / n)
)

obs <- df_data[df_data$observed, ]
miss <- df_data[!df_data$observed, ]

# Target is Jul Y (position 21). With lag = months(7), max_lag = months(18):
# Search window = [target - max_lag, target - lag] = [3, 14] = Jan Y-1 to Dec Y-1
# Note: Nov Y-2 (pos 1) and Dec Y-2 (pos 2) are OUTSIDE the window.
std_win_left <- 3
std_win_right <- 14
target <- 21

# Standard: most recent observed in [3, 14]
# Observed in window: 7, 10, 12, 14 -> most recent = 14 (Dec Y-1)
std_matched <- 14

ff_win_left <- 3
ff_win_right <- 14
ff_matched <- 14

tiles <- function(rows, cx, grp_offset = 0, xsize = ts) {
  do.call(
    rbind,
    lapply(seq_len(nrow(rows)), function(i) {
      data.frame(
        x = cx + c(-1, 1, 1, -1) * xsize / 2,
        y = rows$y[i] + c(-1, -1, 1, 1) * ts / 2,
        group = grp_offset + i,
        alpha = if ("alpha" %in% names(rows)) rows$alpha[i] else NA_real_
      )
    })
  )
}

grp_obs1 <- n
grp_miss1 <- n + nrow(obs)
grp_obs2 <- n + nrow(obs) + nrow(miss)
grp_miss2 <- n + nrow(obs) + nrow(miss) + nrow(obs)

obs1_poly <- tiles(obs, x_std, grp_obs1)
miss1_poly <- tiles(miss, x_std, grp_miss1)
obs2_poly <- tiles(obs, x_ff, grp_obs2)
miss2_poly <- tiles(miss, x_ff, grp_miss2)

# --- Standard grey arrows ----------------------------------------------------
# For each target t in 12..20, find most recent observed in [t-18, t-7]
# Observed positions: 2, 7, 10, 12, 14, 15, 17, 19, 21
# t=20: window [2,13], obs in window: 2,7,10,12   -> 12
# t=19: window [1,12], obs in window: 2,7,10,12   -> 12
# t=18: window [1,11], obs in window: 2,7,10      -> 10
# t=17: window [1,10], obs in window: 2,7,10      -> 10
# t=16: window [1,9],  obs in window: 2,7         -> 7
# t=15: window [1,8],  obs in window: 2,7         -> 7
# t=14: window [1,7],  obs in window: 2,7         -> 7
# t=13: window [1,6],  obs in window: 2           -> 2
# t=12: window [1,5],  obs in window: 2           -> 2
std_grey <- data.frame(
  y = c(20, 19, 18, 17, 16, 15, 14, 13, 12),
  yend = c(12, 12, 10, 10, 7, 7, 7, 2, 2)
)

# --- FF grey arrows ----------------------------------------------------------
# FF candidates (last observed per year): Dec Y-2 (pos 2), Dec Y-1 (pos 14)
# For targets before Jul Y, only Dec Y-2 is in range -> all point to pos 2.
# Jul Y (target) is the first month where Dec Y-1 enters the window -> pos 14.
ff_grey <- data.frame(
  y = c(20, 19, 18, 17, 16, 15, 14, 13, 12),
  yend = c(2, 2, 2, 2, 2, 2, 2, 2, 2)
)

ggplot() +
  # Month timeline: horizontal line with tick marks
  annotate(
    "segment",
    x = x_labels,
    xend = x_labels,
    y = 0.5,
    yend = n + 0.5,
    color = "grey40",
    linewidth = 0.5
  ) +
  annotate(
    "segment",
    x = x_labels - 0.08,
    xend = x_labels + 0.08,
    y = 1:n,
    yend = 1:n,
    color = "grey40",
    linewidth = 0.4
  ) +
  # Month labels: thinned to highlight fiscal-year ends and key markers
  geom_text(
    data = df_data[df_data$y %in% c(2, 5, 8, 11, 14, 17, 20, 21), ],
    aes(x = x_labels - 0.2, y = y, label = label),
    size = 4,
    color = "grey40",
    hjust = 0.5
  ) +
  # --- Standard column: observed ---------------------------------------------
  geom_shape(
    data = obs1_poly,
    aes(x = x, y = y, group = group, alpha = alpha),
    fill = tf_dark_blue,
    color = "white",
    linewidth = 0.8,
    radius = corner
  ) +
  geom_shape(
    data = miss1_poly,
    aes(x = x, y = y, group = group),
    fill = "grey97",
    color = "grey80",
    linewidth = 0.8,
    radius = corner
  ) +
  geom_text(
    data = miss,
    aes(x = x_std, y = y),
    label = "NA",
    size = 3.2,
    color = "grey65",
    fontface = "italic"
  ) +
  # --- FF column: observed ---------------------------------------------------
  geom_shape(
    data = obs2_poly,
    aes(x = x, y = y, group = group, alpha = alpha),
    fill = tf_dark_blue,
    color = "white",
    linewidth = 0.8,
    radius = corner
  ) +
  geom_shape(
    data = miss2_poly,
    aes(x = x, y = y, group = group),
    fill = "grey97",
    color = "grey80",
    linewidth = 0.8,
    radius = corner
  ) +
  geom_text(
    data = miss,
    aes(x = x_ff, y = y),
    label = "NA",
    size = 3.2,
    color = "grey65",
    fontface = "italic"
  ) +
  # --- Standard grey arrows --------------------------------------------------
  geom_curve(
    data = data.frame(
      x = x_std + ts / 2,
      xend = x_std + ts / 2,
      y = std_grey$y,
      yend = std_grey$yend + 0.15
    ),
    aes(x = x, y = y, xend = xend, yend = yend),
    curvature = -0.2,
    color = "grey70",
    alpha = 0.5,
    arrow = arrow(length = unit(0.08, "cm"), type = "closed"),
    linewidth = 0.35
  ) +
  # Standard search window
  annotate(
    "rect",
    xmin = x_std - ts / 2 - win_pad,
    xmax = x_std + ts / 2 + win_pad,
    ymin = std_win_left - ts / 2 - win_pad,
    ymax = std_win_right + ts / 2 + win_pad,
    fill = NA,
    color = tf_yellow,
    linewidth = 0.9,
    linetype = "dashed"
  ) +
  annotate(
    "text",
    x = x_std - ts / 2 - win_pad - 0.2,
    y = c(std_win_left - ts / 2 - win_pad, std_win_right + ts / 2 + win_pad),
    label = c("max_lag", "lag"),
    color = tf_yellow,
    size = 3.4,
    fontface = "italic",
    hjust = -0.2,
    vjust = 0.5
  ) +
  # Standard highlighted arrow: Jul Y -> Dec Y-1
  annotate(
    "curve",
    x = x_std + ts / 2,
    xend = x_std + ts / 2,
    y = target,
    yend = std_matched + 0.2,
    curvature = -0.2,
    color = tf_dark_blue,
    linewidth = 0.9,
    arrow = arrow(length = unit(0.14, "cm"), type = "closed")
  ) +
  # --- FF grey arrows --------------------------------------------------------
  geom_curve(
    data = data.frame(
      x = x_ff + ts / 2,
      xend = x_ff + ts / 2,
      y = ff_grey$y,
      yend = ff_grey$yend + 0.15
    ),
    aes(x = x, y = y, xend = xend, yend = yend),
    curvature = -0.2,
    color = "grey70",
    alpha = 0.5,
    arrow = arrow(length = unit(0.08, "cm"), type = "closed"),
    linewidth = 0.35
  ) +
  # FF search window
  annotate(
    "rect",
    xmin = x_ff - ts / 2 - win_pad,
    xmax = x_ff + ts / 2 + win_pad,
    ymin = ff_win_left - ts / 2 - win_pad,
    ymax = ff_win_right + ts / 2 + win_pad,
    fill = NA,
    color = tf_yellow,
    linewidth = 0.9,
    linetype = "dashed"
  ) +
  annotate(
    "text",
    x = x_ff - ts / 2 - win_pad - 0.2,
    y = c(ff_win_left - ts / 2 - win_pad, ff_win_right + ts / 2 + win_pad),
    label = c("max_lag", "lag"),
    color = tf_yellow,
    size = 3.4,
    fontface = "italic",
    hjust = -0.2,
    vjust = 0.5
  ) +
  # FF highlighted arrow: Jul Y -> Dec Y-1
  annotate(
    "curve",
    x = x_ff + ts / 2,
    xend = x_ff + ts / 2,
    y = target,
    yend = ff_matched + 0.2,
    curvature = -0.2,
    color = tf_dark_blue,
    linewidth = 0.9,
    arrow = arrow(length = unit(0.14, "cm"), type = "closed")
  ) +
  # --- Main title (bold) -----------------------------------------------------
  annotate(
    "text",
    x = max(x_std, x_ff) + ts / 2 + 1.0,
    y = n / 2,
    label = "data |> add_lagged_columns(lag = months(7), max_lag = months(18))",
    color = "black",
    size = 3.2,
    family = "mono",
    fontface = "bold",
    hjust = 0.5
  ) +
  # --- Panel headers (above each panel of tiles) -----------------------------
  annotate(
    "text",
    x = x_std + ts / 2 + 0.35,
    y = 0.1,
    label = "Panel A",
    color = "grey30",
    size = 3.6,
    fontface = "bold",
    hjust = 0
  ) +
  annotate(
    "text",
    x = x_ff + ts / 2 + 0.35,
    y = 0.1,
    label = "Panel B",
    color = "grey30",
    size = 3.6,
    fontface = "bold",
    hjust = 0
  ) +
  # --- Panel labels (left margin, rotated, bold) -----------------------------
  # Inner labels: TRUE / FALSE for each panel
  annotate(
    "text",
    x = x_std,
    y = -0.1,
    label = "FALSE",
    color = "grey30",
    size = 4.0,
    family = "mono",
    fontface = "bold",
    angle = 90,
    hjust = 0.5,
    vjust = 0.5
  ) +
  annotate(
    "text",
    x = x_ff,
    y = -0.1,
    label = "TRUE",
    color = "grey30",
    size = 4.0,
    family = "mono",
    fontface = "bold",
    angle = 90,
    hjust = 0.5,
    vjust = 0.5
  ) +
  # Outer label spanning both panels
  annotate(
    "text",
    x = (x_std + x_ff) / 2,
    y = -0.8,
    label = "ff_adjustment",
    color = "grey30",
    size = 4.0,
    family = "mono",
    fontface = "bold",
    angle = 90,
    hjust = 0.5,
    vjust = 0.5
  ) +
  # --- Year-change dashed lines (SHORTENED) ----------------------------------
  # Now stop at the right edge of the yellow search window rather than extending
  # all the way across to the title area. This removes the long dashes cluttering
  # the top of the figure.
  # Between Dec Y-2 (pos 2) and Jan Y-1 (pos 3): line at 2.5
  # Between Dec Y-1 (pos 14) and Jan Y (pos 15): line at 14.5
  annotate(
    "segment",
    x = x_labels - 0.55,
    xend = x_std + ts / 2 + 0.7,
    y = 2.5,
    yend = 2.5,
    color = "grey30",
    linewidth = 0.5,
    linetype = "dashed"
  ) +
  annotate(
    "segment",
    x = x_labels - 0.55,
    xend = x_std + ts / 2 + 0.7,
    y = 14.5,
    yend = 14.5,
    color = "grey30",
    linewidth = 0.5,
    linetype = "dashed"
  ) +
  # --- Year span brackets ----------------------------------------------------
  # Year T-2:  pos 1 to 2   (Nov-Dec Y-2)
  # Year T-1:  pos 3 to 14  (Jan-Dec Y-1)
  # Year T:    pos 15 to 21 (Jan-Jul Y)
  annotate(
    "segment",
    x = x_labels - 0.55,
    xend = x_labels - 0.55,
    y = c(1, 3, 15),
    yend = c(2, 14, 21),
    color = "grey30",
    linewidth = 0.4
  ) +
  # Bracket end caps
  annotate(
    "segment",
    x = x_labels - 0.50,
    xend = x_labels - 0.60,
    y = c(1, 2, 3, 14, 15, 21),
    yend = c(1, 2, 3, 14, 15, 21),
    color = "grey30",
    linewidth = 0.4
  ) +
  # Year labels at midpoints:
  # Year T-2: midpoint of [1, 2] = 1.5
  # Year T-1: midpoint of [3, 14] = 8.5
  # Year T:   midpoint of [15, 21] = 18
  annotate(
    "text",
    x = x_labels - 0.75,
    y = c(1.5, 8.5, 18),
    label = c("Year T-2", "Year T-1", "Year T"),
    color = "grey30",
    size = 4.0,
    fontface = "bold"
  ) +
  scale_alpha_identity() +
  scale_x_continuous(
    limits = c(x_labels - 1.15, max(x_std, x_ff) + ts / 2 + 1.3),
    expand = c(0, 0)
  ) +
  scale_y_continuous(
    limits = c(-1.0, n + 0.55),
    expand = c(0, 0)
  ) +
  coord_flip() +
  theme_void() +
  theme(plot.margin = margin(5, 10, 5, 10))
```

A handful of additional helpers cover routine operations that recur across empirical studies. `winsorize()` and `trim()` handle outliers in cross-sectional variables: the former symmetrically replaces values below the $q$-th and above the $(1-q)$-th percentile with the corresponding quantile values, while the latter sets them to `NA`. `estimate_model()` fits a linear model from a formula string and returns the coefficients as a tidy one-row data frame, which composes naturally with `group_by()` for grouped or rolling regressions such as estimating time-series factor exposures stock by stock. `compute_rolling_value()` applies an arbitrary aggregation function over a rolling window defined in calendar time rather than row counts, accommodating irregular observation frequencies and missing periods.

### Portfolio sorting {#sec-portfolio-sorting}

A portfolio sort groups stocks each period into ordered portfolios according to the level of a sorting variable. The boundaries between portfolios are called *breakpoints*: numeric cutoffs of the sorting variable that determine which portfolio a stock joins. A quintile sort on size, for instance, has four breakpoints at the 20th, 40th, 60th, and 80th percentiles of the cross-sectional market-capitalization distribution. Common sorting variables include size, beta, book-to-market, and momentum. The long-short return between the extreme portfolios is interpreted as a factor-mimicking strategy and serves as the basis for tests of whether the sorting variable forecasts future returns. Portfolio sorts are among the most widely used tools in empirical asset pricing [@bali.2016]. We expose the procedure through four composable building blocks plus a one-call wrapper.

`compute_breakpoints()` takes a cross-section and a sorting variable and returns the numeric cutoffs that define the portfolio boundaries. The user supplies either a number of portfolios (for example, five for quintiles) or an explicit vector of percentiles, but not both. A `breakpoints_exchanges` argument restricts the universe used to compute breakpoints. The standard convention is NYSE listed stocks only, which prevents the large cross-section of small NASDAQ firms from dominating the lower bins [@jensen.2023]. A related `breakpoints_min_size_threshold` argument excludes stocks below a market-cap quantile from the breakpoint computation, which size-related sorts often require because microcaps would otherwise distort the cutoffs. A `smooth_bunching` flag handles cases where the sorting variable takes the same value for many observations at the bottom or top of the distribution, so that the lowest (or highest) two quantile breakpoints coincide. Without intervention, all tied observations would land in a single boundary portfolio while neighboring portfolios remain empty. When `smooth_bunching = TRUE`, the function assigns the bunched observations to the boundary portfolio and recomputes the remaining breakpoints on the subset of observations strictly inside the boundary value, restoring well-defined cutoffs for the interior portfolios.

`assign_portfolio()` maps each observation to a portfolio integer and uses breakpoints supplied either directly or via a breakpoint-computing function (defaulting to `compute_breakpoints()`). In practice, `assign_portfolio()` is called separately for each rebalancing date, so that portfolios are reformed each period rather than fixed once for the whole sample.

`compute_portfolio_returns()` ties the lower-level pieces together. Given a panel of stock data, one or two sorting variables, a sorting method, and `breakpoint_options`, it handles rebalancing, breakpoint computation, portfolio assignment, and return aggregation. It then returns a complete panel of portfolio returns. For each portfolio-date the function reports three return measures: equal-weighted, value-weighted using `mktcap_lag` as the weight, and capped value-weighted [@jensen.2023]. The capped version pulls weights above the `cap_weight` percentile (default `0.8` corresponds to $80\%$) back to that cap, which prevents a small number of megacap firms from dominating the portfolio. A `min_portfolio_size` argument sets the minimum number of constituents below which the corresponding return is set to `NA`. An optional `rebalancing_month` argument switches from period-by-period rebalancing to annual rebalancing in the specified month. Portfolios formed in that month are then held constant for the following twelve months.

The function supports three sorting schemes, illustrated in @fig-illustrate-portfolio-helper. A *univariate* sort uses a single variable. An *independent bivariate* sort computes breakpoints on each variable separately and intersects the resulting bins to produce a two-way grid. A *dependent bivariate* sort first partitions the cross-section by the secondary (control) variable and then re-sorts within each bucket on the main variable, which is the appropriate choice when the second variable is treated as a control rather than as an independent dimension of variation. For bivariate sorts, returns are averaged over the secondary variable so that only the main-variable portfolios are returned.

```{r}
#| label: illustrate-portfolio-helper
#| echo: false
set.seed(3010)

n <- 1000
rho <- 0.6

# shared signal
f <- rnorm(n)

# independent noise
e1 <- rnorm(n)
e2 <- rnorm(n)

# construct correlated latent variables
x1 <- f + sqrt(1 - rho^2) * e1
x2 <- f + sqrt(1 - rho^2) * e2

# map to (0,1)
asset_growth <- pnorm(x1)
mktcap_lag <- pnorm(x2)

cross_section <- data.frame(asset_growth, mktcap_lag)
n_portfolio <- 2

breakpoints_ag <- cross_section |>
  compute_breakpoints(
    "asset_growth",
    breakpoint_options = breakpoint_options(n_portfolios = n_portfolio)
  )

portfolios_univariate <- cross_section |>
  dplyr::mutate(
    ag_portfolio = assign_portfolio(
      pick(everything()),
      "asset_growth",
      breakpoint_options = breakpoint_options(n_portfolios = n_portfolio)
    )
  )

portfolios_independent <- cross_section |>
  dplyr::mutate(
    ag_portfolio = assign_portfolio(
      pick(everything()),
      "asset_growth",
      breakpoint_options = breakpoint_options(n_portfolios = n_portfolio)
    ),
    size_portfolio = assign_portfolio(
      dplyr::pick(everything()),
      "mktcap_lag",
      breakpoint_options = breakpoint_options(n_portfolios = n_portfolio)
    ),
    portfolio_cell = paste0(ag_portfolio, "-", size_portfolio)
  )

portfolios_dependent <- cross_section |>
  dplyr::mutate(
    size_portfolio = assign_portfolio(
      dplyr::pick(everything()),
      "mktcap_lag",
      breakpoint_options = breakpoint_options(n_portfolios = n_portfolio)
    )
  ) |>
  dplyr::group_by(size_portfolio) |>
  dplyr::mutate(
    ag_portfolio = assign_portfolio(
      dplyr::pick(everything()),
      "asset_growth",
      breakpoint_options = breakpoint_options(n_portfolios = n_portfolio)
    ),
    portfolio_cell = paste0(ag_portfolio, "-", size_portfolio)
  ) |>
  dplyr::ungroup()
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-illustrate-portfolio-helper
#| echo: false
#| fig-cap: !expr 'paste0("Portfolio sort approaches illustrated on a simulated cross-section. Each panel plots simulated observations assigned to ", n_portfolio, " × ", n_portfolio, " portfolios based on asset growth rank (x-axis) and size rank (y-axis), both expressed as percentiles. Colors indicate portfolio cell assignment. The univariate sort (left) assigns portfolios on asset growth alone; the independent bivariate sort (center) assigns each dimension independently; the dependent bivariate sort (right) sorts on size first, then on asset growth within size groups.")'
#| fig-width: 6.5
#| out-width: "100%"
common_theme <- list(
  scale_x_continuous(
    labels = scales::percent,
    breaks = breakpoints_ag,
    expand = c(0.01, 0)
  ),
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::percent, expand = c(0.01, 0)),
  labs(x = "Asset growth rank", y = "Size rank"),
  theme(
    panel.grid = element_blank(),
    plot.title = element_text(hjust = 0),
    plot.title.position = "plot"
  )
)

p1 <- portfolios_univariate |>
  ggplot(aes(
    x = asset_growth,
    y = mktcap_lag,
    color = as.factor(ag_portfolio)
  )) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.4, size = 0.8) +
  labs(title = "Univariate sort") +
  common_theme

p2 <- portfolios_independent |>
  ggplot(aes(x = asset_growth, y = mktcap_lag, color = portfolio_cell)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.4, size = 0.8) +
  labs(title = "Independent\nbivariate sort") +
  common_theme

p3 <- portfolios_dependent |>
  ggplot(aes(x = asset_growth, y = mktcap_lag, color = portfolio_cell)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.4, size = 0.8) +
  labs(title = "Dependent\nbivariate sort") +
  common_theme

p1 +
  p2 +
  p3 +
  plot_layout(guides = "collect", axes = "collect_y") +
  plot_annotation(
    title = "Portfolio sort approaches",
    subtitle = paste0(
      "Simulated cross-section: ",
      n_portfolio,
      "×",
      n_portfolio,
      " portfolios"
    ),
    theme = theme(
      plot.title = element_text(face = "bold"),
      plot.title.position = "plot"
    )
  )
```

`compute_long_short_returns()` takes the output of `compute_portfolio_returns()` and computes the spread between the top and bottom portfolios. A `direction` argument controls the sign and defaults to `"top_minus_bottom"`. The function returns one long-short series per return measure available in the input, so the equal-weighted, value-weighted, and capped value-weighted spreads are produced together. This long-short return is the factor-mimicking spread that the asset-pricing literature typically takes as the object of interest.

For users who want the full pipeline in a single call, `implement_portfolio_sort()` wraps the four functions above. It takes a panel of stock data, one or two sorting variables, a sorting method, and a configuration object, and returns the long-short factor return series alongside the underlying portfolio returns. The lower-level functions remain available for custom workflows that need finer control over breakpoints, weighting, or rebalancing.

## A case study in factor construction {#sec-ag}

We walk through the construction of the asset growth factor from raw CRSP and Compustat data to long-short portfolio returns, applying each stage of @tbl-functions in turn.

Load [tidyfinance]{.pkg} together with a minimal set of supporting packages: [dplyr]{.pkg} [@dplyr] for data manipulation, [tidyr]{.pkg} [@tidyr] for reshaping between long and wide formats, and [lubridate]{.pkg} [@lubridate] for date arithmetic.

```{r}
#| label: load-package
#| message: false
#| warning: false
#| cache: false
library("tidyfinance")
library("dplyr")
library("tidyr")
library("lubridate")
```

### Data download {#sec-data-download}

Constructing the asset growth factor requires two WRDS panels: annual accounting data from Compustat to compute the asset growth signal and monthly stock returns from CRSP to translate the signal into portfolio returns.

CRSP and Compustat are proprietary and require a WRDS subscription. All numbers, tables, and figures in this paper are computed from the real WRDS data with `data_domain <- "wrds"`. Readers without a WRDS subscription can render the entire manuscript against synthetic data of identical schema by setting `data_domain <- "pseudo"` in the chunk below. The pseudo path covers the four WRDS-sourced datasets the case study consumes: daily and monthly CRSP returns, quarterly and annual Compustat fundamentals, and the CRSP-Compustat linking table. Every `download_data()` call for one of these datasets then routes to an in-package synthetic generator rather than to WRDS, so the document compiles end-to-end without a subscription, credentials, or network access to a paid provider.

The generator preserves column names, dtypes, missingness patterns, panel structure, and approximate scales, so the cleaning, lagging, and sorting code paths exercise the same branches they would on real data, and every figure and table in this paper renders without error. What the generator does not preserve are economic relationships. Returns are independent draws around a calibrated mean, and characteristics carry no predictive content for subsequent returns; the long-short premia recovered against pseudo data are therefore noise. The workflow reproduces; the quantitative results do not.

Two arguments to `download_data()` control the synthetic draws: `seed` fixes the random number generator so that two readers running the same chunk obtain bit-identical pseudo panels, and `n_assets` sets the size of the synthetic cross-section (default `1000L`), trading off compile speed against the realism of cross-sectional statistics. The practical implication is that every chunk in this paper can be inspected, edited, and re-rendered on a laptop with no proprietary data and no credentials; only the headline factor premia require WRDS to reproduce numerically.

Before the first WRDS download, call `set_wrds_credentials()` to store WRDS credentials securely in `.Renviron`; subsequent `download_data()` calls establish the database connection automatically.

```{r}
#| label: set-data-domain
data_domain <- "wrds"
```

```{r}
#| label: set-date-range
date_start <- as.Date("1972-01-01")
date_end <- as.Date("2024-12-31")
```

We restrict the sample to the period from `{r} year(date_start)` onward because Compustat coverage is often incomplete before that date, and we end the sample at `{r} year(date_end)`, the most recent full calendar year at the time of writing.

First, we download monthly stock returns from CRSP. Setting `add_ccm_links = TRUE` appends CRSP-Compustat linking identifiers needed to merge with financial statement data in the next step.

```{r}
#| label: download-crsp
crsp_monthly <- download_data(
  domain = data_domain,
  dataset = "crsp_monthly",
  version = "v2",
  start_date = date_start,
  end_date = date_end,
  add_ccm_links = TRUE
)
```

The dataset contains `{r} format(nrow(crsp_monthly), big.mark = ",")` stock-month observations for `{r} format(length(unique(crsp_monthly$permno)), big.mark = ",")` unique stocks, covering the period from `{r} format_pretty_date(min(crsp_monthly$date))` to `{r} format_pretty_date(max(crsp_monthly$date))`.

Next, we download annual financial statements from Compustat.

```{r}
#| label: download-compustat
compustat_annual <- download_data(
  domain = data_domain,
  dataset = "compustat_annual",
  start_date = date_start,
  end_date = date_end,
  additional_columns = c("at", "ib"),
  only_usd = TRUE
) |>
  select(gvkey, date, at, ib)
```

Annual Compustat data contain `{r} format(nrow(compustat_annual), big.mark = ",")` firm-year observations for `{r} format(length(unique(compustat_annual$gvkey)), big.mark = ",")` unique firms, covering the period from `{r} format_pretty_date(date_start)` to `{r} format_pretty_date(date_end)`. The `additional_columns` argument retrieves total assets (`at`) and income before extraordinary items (`ib`), needed for computing asset growth and applying an earnings filter in later steps. Setting `only_usd = TRUE` restricts the dataset to USD-denominated stocks, ensuring consistency with CRSP.

### Data cleaning and variable construction {#sec-data-cleaning}

We illustrate data cleaning and variable construction using asset growth (AG) as our running example. Asset growth is the year-over-year percentage change in total assets [@cooper.2008],

$$
AG_t = (AT_t - AT_{t-1}) / AT_{t-1},
$$

where $AT_t$ is total assets in year $t$ (Compustat field `at`).

The `add_lagged_columns()` function from [tidyfinance]{.pkg} handles temporal alignment by creating a lagged version of total assets grouped by firm identifier (`gvkey`) with a one-year lag. Non-finite values (arising when lagged total assets are zero or missing) become `NA`.

```{r}
#| label: compute-sorting-variables
sorting_variable_data <- compustat_annual |>
  add_lagged_columns(
    cols = "at",
    lag = years(1),
    by = "gvkey"
  ) |>
  mutate(
    asset_growth = (at - at_lag) / at_lag,
    asset_growth = if_else(is.finite(asset_growth), asset_growth, NA_real_)
  ) |>
  select(gvkey, date, asset_growth, ib)
```

The call relies on two silent defaults: `max_lag` falls back to `lag` (here one year), so only the single observation exactly one year before each row is eligible; `ff_adjustment = FALSE`, so the look-back is the plain calendar window rather than the Fama-French June/July rebalancing convention introduced in @sec-variable-construction.

`sorting_variable_data` contains one observation per firm-year, the natural unit for cross-sectional analysis of annual accounting variables. Asset growth is heavily right-skewed: a small number of firms with dramatic balance-sheet expansions generate extreme positive values. @tbl-ag-summary reports the pooled cross-sectional summary alongside the time-series average, minimum, and maximum of the corresponding statistic computed cross-sectionally each year.^[The pooled count of `{r} format(sum(!is.na(sorting_variable_data$asset_growth)), big.mark = ",")` firm-years is below the `{r} format(nrow(compustat_annual), big.mark = ",")` downloaded in @sec-data-download because the one-year lag in the asset-growth construction drops each firm's first observation.] We obtain both views with `create_summary_statistics()`, a [tidyfinance]{.pkg} helper that returns the standard set of cross-sectional summary statistics for a variable: applied to the pooled (winsorized) sample for the first column and grouped by calendar year for the next three. @tbl-ag-summary assembles the two computations side by side.

```{r}
#| label: ag-summary-prep
pooled_stats <- sorting_variable_data |>
  drop_na(asset_growth) |>
  mutate(asset_growth = winsorize(asset_growth, 0.01)) |>
  create_summary_statistics(asset_growth, detail = TRUE)
yearly_stats <- sorting_variable_data |>
  drop_na(asset_growth) |>
  group_by(year = year(date)) |>
  mutate(asset_growth = winsorize(asset_growth, 0.01)) |>
  ungroup() |>
  create_summary_statistics(asset_growth, by = year, detail = TRUE)
```

```{r}
#| label: tbl-ag-summary
#| tbl-cap: !expr 'paste0("Cross-sectional summary statistics for asset growth (winsorized at the 1st and 99th percentiles). The ''Pooled'' column reports the statistic computed on the entire firm-year sample. The ''Yearly'' columns summarize the time series of statistic values computed cross-sectionally year by year, taking the average, minimum, and maximum across calendar years. N is the count of firm-year observations (pooled) or per-year observations (yearly columns). Sample: ", year(date_start), "--", year(date_end), ".")'
#| echo: false
stat_cols <- c("n", "mean", "sd", "q10", "q25", "q50", "q75", "q90")
stat_labels <- c("N", "Mean", "SD", "P10", "P25", "Median", "P75", "P90")
fmt_val <- function(col, x) {
  if (col == "n") {
    formatC(round(x), format = "d", big.mark = ",")
  } else {
    formatC(x, format = "f", digits = 3)
  }
}

tibble::tibble(
  Statistic = stat_labels,
  Pooled = vapply(
    stat_cols,
    function(s) fmt_val(s, pooled_stats[[s]]),
    character(1)
  ),
  `Yearly avg` = vapply(
    stat_cols,
    function(s) fmt_val(s, mean(yearly_stats[[s]])),
    character(1)
  ),
  `Yearly min` = vapply(
    stat_cols,
    function(s) fmt_val(s, min(yearly_stats[[s]])),
    character(1)
  ),
  `Yearly max` = vapply(
    stat_cols,
    function(s) fmt_val(s, max(yearly_stats[[s]])),
    character(1)
  )
) |>
  knitr::kable(
    align = "lrrrr",
    format = "latex",
    booktabs = TRUE,
    linesep = ""
  )
```

The next step merges annual sorting variables onto the monthly CRSP stock panel using `join_lagged_values()`. The function aligns fiscal-year-end data with monthly observations through a configurable lag window. Setting `ff_adjustment = TRUE` implements the Fama-French convention [@fama.1993], aligning fiscal-year data from year $t$ with portfolio formation in July of year $t+1$ through a 12-to-18-month look-back window.

```{r}
#| label: lag-sorting-variables
sorting_data <- crsp_monthly |>
  join_lagged_values(
    new_data = sorting_variable_data,
    id_keys = "gvkey",
    min_lag = months(7),
    max_lag = months(18),
    ff_adjustment = TRUE
  ) |>
  select(
    date,
    permno,
    exchange,
    siccd,
    ret_excess,
    mktcap_lag,
    asset_growth,
    ib
  ) |>
  filter(date > date_start + months(12) + months(18))
```

The filter removes the initial year used to compute the growth rate plus an additional 18 months to avoid mechanically introduced gaps from the lagging step, leaving a panel of stock-month observations with excess returns, exchange membership, lagged market capitalization, and the lagged sorting variable. The auxiliary columns `siccd` and `ib` support the sample-construction filters in @sec-customized-sorts.

@fig-ag-percentiles shows the 33rd, 50th, and 66th percentiles of asset growth over time in the resulting panel; pronounced spikes during economic expansions and contractions highlight the cyclical nature of corporate investment that portfolio sorts aim to exploit.

```{r}
#| label: fig-ag-percentiles
#| fig-cap: !expr 'paste0("Selected percentiles (33rd, 50th, 66th) of cross-sectional asset growth over time. The y-axis reports annual growth in total assets in percent. Sample: ", year(date_start), "--", year(date_end), ".")'
#| fig-width: 6.5
#| out-width: "100%"
#| echo: false
plot_data <- sorting_data |>
  drop_na() |>
  group_by(date) |>
  summarize(
    "33%" = quantile(asset_growth, 0.33),
    "Median" = quantile(asset_growth, 0.50),
    "66%" = quantile(asset_growth, 0.66),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) |>
  pivot_longer(
    cols = -date,
    names_to = "quantile",
    values_to = "asset_growth"
  )

label_data <- plot_data |>
  group_by(quantile) |>
  slice_max(date, n = 1) |>
  mutate(date = date %m+% months(6)) |> # Nudge labels right of the last observation
  ungroup()

ggplot(plot_data, aes(x = date, y = asset_growth, color = quantile)) +
  geom_line() +
  geom_text(
    data = label_data,
    aes(label = quantile),
    hjust = 0,
    show.legend = FALSE
  ) +
  scale_x_date(expand = expansion(mult = c(0.02, 0.12))) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::percent) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Asset growth") +
  theme(legend.position = "none")
```

With the sorting variable constructed and merged onto the monthly stock panel, we now turn to portfolio sorts, the mechanism that translates firm-level characteristics into tradable factor returns.

### Portfolio sorts {#sec-portfolio-sorts}

In portfolio sorts, stocks are ranked each period by their sorting variable and divided into quantile portfolios. Portfolio returns are equal-weighted or value-weighted averages of constituent stock returns. The long-short factor return is the difference between the extreme portfolios. For asset growth, the relevant spread is bottom minus top, reflecting the negative premium documented by @cooper.2008. The construction involves several methodological choices: which stocks enter the universe, how many portfolios to form, which exchange determines the breakpoints, the weighting scheme, and the rebalancing frequency.

`implement_portfolio_sort()` exposes all of these choices through a single function call. The function takes the panel data, one or two sorting variables, a sorting method, and a `portfolio_sort_options` object that bundles two configuration layers: `filter_options()` controls which observations enter the breakpoint and return computation (for example, excluding financial firms or stocks below a minimum price), and `breakpoint_options()` controls how portfolios are formed (number of portfolios, exchange universe, bunching). Internally, the function applies the sample filters and then calls `compute_portfolio_returns()`, which produces the time series of portfolio returns. A subsequent call to `compute_long_short_returns()` constructs the long-short portfolio.

`compute_portfolio_returns()` itself rests on two lower-level helpers, `compute_breakpoints()` for quantile cutoffs and `assign_portfolio()` for mapping each stock-month to a portfolio number. Both are exported, so researchers who need finer control can call them directly rather than through the wrapper. The two examples below use `implement_portfolio_sort()` throughout.

#### Baseline specification (univariate sorts) {#sec-baseline-sorts}

The simplest call to `implement_portfolio_sort()` requires only a `portfolio_sort_options` object that specifies how to form the breakpoints. In a univariate sort, stocks are ranked on a single characteristic. We illustrate using asset growth as the sorting variable, forming quintile portfolios with breakpoints computed from NYSE-listed stocks only, and rebalancing annually in July.

```{r}
#| label: baseline-options
options_baseline <- portfolio_sort_options(
  breakpoint_options_main = breakpoint_options(
    n_portfolios = 5,
    breakpoints_exchanges = "NYSE"
  )
)
```

The `breakpoint_options()` call specifies that breakpoints come from NYSE-listed stocks only, a common convention that avoids the influence of small AMEX and NASDAQ firms on portfolio cutoffs. We then pass these options to `implement_portfolio_sort()`.

```{r}
#| label: baseline-sort
portfolio_returns <- implement_portfolio_sort(
  data = sorting_data,
  sorting_variables = "asset_growth",
  sorting_method = "univariate",
  rebalancing_month = 7,
  portfolio_sort_options = options_baseline
)
```

Apart from setting `rebalancing_month = 7`, every other choice point falls back to the package default: a cap-weight cutoff at the 80th percentile of market capitalization for the capped value-weighted return, no minimum portfolio size, and no smooth bunching. The standard CRSP/Compustat column names (`permno`, `date`, `ret_excess`, `mktcap_lag`, `exchange`) are picked up automatically through the default `data_options()`. Setting `rebalancing_month = 7` reforms the portfolios each July and holds them for the following twelve months, the standard Fama-French rebalancing convention. This pairs with `ff_adjustment = TRUE` in `join_lagged_values()`: the signal is locked in at the June/July boundary, so July is the first month in which a fresh fiscal-year update is available.

`compute_portfolio_returns()`, called internally, returns a long tibble with one row per portfolio-month and the three weighting columns introduced in @sec-portfolio-sorting: `ret_excess_vw` (value-weighted, VW), `ret_excess_ew` (equal-weighted, EW), and `ret_excess_vw_capped` (capped value-weighted, VWC). Piping the result through `compute_long_short_returns()` gives the long-short portfolio. The `direction = "bottom_minus_top"` argument means the factor is long low-AG stocks and short high-AG stocks, in line with the negative premium documented by @cooper.2008.

```{r}
#| label: long-short-ag
factor_returns_ag <- portfolio_returns |>
  compute_long_short_returns(direction = "bottom_minus_top")
```

@tbl-univariate-sort-ag summarizes the time series of each quintile across all three weighting schemes, with the long-short portfolio appended as the final row.

```{r}
#| label: univariate-sort-ag-stats
return_summary <- function(data) {
  data |>
    drop_na() |>
    summarize(
      across(
        c(ret_excess_vw, ret_excess_ew, ret_excess_vw_capped),
        list(
          mean = \(x) mean(x) * 12,
          tstat = \(x) mean(x) / (sd(x) / sqrt(n()))
        ),
        .names = "{.col}_{.fn}"
      ),
      .groups = "drop"
    )
}
univariate_sort_table <- bind_rows(
  portfolio_returns |>
    group_by(portfolio) |>
    return_summary() |>
    mutate(portfolio = as.character(portfolio)),
  factor_returns_ag |>
    return_summary() |>
    mutate(portfolio = "L/S")
)
```

```{=latex}
\begingroup
\small
```

```{r}
#| label: tbl-univariate-sort-ag
#| tbl-cap: !expr 'paste0("Time-series averages of annualized monthly excess returns for asset growth quintile portfolios. Portfolios are formed annually in July using NYSE breakpoints. Means are annualized (multiplied by 12). The $t$~statistic tests whether the mean monthly excess return differs from zero. Capped value-weighted pulls weights above the 80th percentile back to that cap. The L/S row is the long-short portfolio (bottom minus top quintile). Sample: ", year(date_start), "--", year(date_end), ".")'
#| echo: false
group_header <- paste0(
  " & \\multicolumn{2}{c}{Value-weighted} & ",
  "\\multicolumn{2}{c}{Equal-weighted} & ",
  "\\multicolumn{2}{c}{Capped value-weighted} \\\\\n",
  "\\cmidrule(lr){2-3} \\cmidrule(lr){4-5} \\cmidrule(lr){6-7}\n"
)

raw_table <- univariate_sort_table |>
  knitr::kable(
    digits = 3,
    escape = FALSE,
    format = "latex",
    booktabs = TRUE,
    linesep = "",
    col.names = c(
      "Portfolio",
      "Mean",
      "$t$~statistic",
      "Mean",
      "$t$~statistic",
      "Mean",
      "$t$~statistic"
    )
  )

structure(
  sub(
    "\\toprule\n",
    paste0("\\toprule\n", group_header),
    raw_table,
    fixed = TRUE
  ),
  format = attr(raw_table, "format"),
  class = class(raw_table)
)
```

```{=latex}
\endgroup
```

The value-weighted long-short portfolio earns `{r} round(mean(factor_returns_ag$ret_excess_vw, na.rm = TRUE) * 12 * 100, 1)`% per year ($t$~statistic of `{r} round(mean(factor_returns_ag$ret_excess_vw, na.rm = TRUE) / (sd(factor_returns_ag$ret_excess_vw, na.rm = TRUE) / sqrt(sum(!is.na(factor_returns_ag$ret_excess_vw)))), 2)`), consistent with the negative premium documented by @cooper.2008. The equal-weighted spread is larger, as expected for characteristics that correlate with size. The monotone decline of value-weighted means across quintiles confirms that [tidyfinance]{.pkg} reproduces the literature result from raw WRDS data with a single function call.

#### Customized specification (bivariate sorts) {#sec-customized-sorts}

The baseline specification above takes nearly every package default and runs a univariate sort to form long-short portfolios. The customized specification below changes both: it overrides several of those defaults through `portfolio_sort_options` and moves from sorting on one variable to sorting on two.

We adopt a specification that combines, in a single call to `implement_portfolio_sort()`, the universe restrictions and breakpoint conventions used in many empirical studies: exclude financials and utilities, exclude firms with non-positive earnings, ignore the smallest 20% of NYSE-listed firms when computing breakpoints, form quintiles on AG within size buckets, use NYSE-only breakpoints, rebalance annually in July, and require at least ten constituents per portfolio.

Bivariate (double) sorts control for a second variable, typically firm size (`mktcap_lag`), when forming portfolios on the main characteristic. We use the dependent variant introduced in @sec-portfolio-sorting and illustrated in @fig-illustrate-portfolio-helper: stocks are first split into size buckets, then sorted into asset growth portfolios within each bucket, with returns averaged across the size dimension.

```{r}
#| label: customized-options
options_customized <- portfolio_sort_options(
  filter_options = filter_options(
    exclude_financials = TRUE,
    exclude_utilities = TRUE,
    exclude_negative_earnings = TRUE
  ),
  breakpoint_options_main = breakpoint_options(
    n_portfolios = 5,
    breakpoints_exchanges = "NYSE",
    breakpoints_min_size_threshold = 0.2
  ),
  breakpoint_options_secondary = breakpoint_options(
    n_portfolios = 2,
    breakpoints_exchanges = "NYSE"
  )
)
```

```{r}
#| label: customized-sort
portfolio_returns_customized <- implement_portfolio_sort(
  data = sorting_data,
  sorting_variables = c("asset_growth", "mktcap_lag"),
  sorting_method = "bivariate-dependent",
  rebalancing_month = 7,
  portfolio_sort_options = options_customized,
  min_portfolio_size = 10,
  quiet = TRUE
)
factor_returns_customized <- portfolio_returns_customized |>
  compute_long_short_returns(direction = "bottom_minus_top")
```

A single options object (`options_customized`) bundles every methodological choice that distinguishes this specification from the baseline; nothing in the surrounding pipeline changes. Switching from a univariate to a size-controlled dependent double sort is a one-word change in `sorting_method`, and the secondary breakpoint object is supplied alongside the primary one without any additional work. Setting `quiet = TRUE` suppresses the diagnostic messages from `filter_sorting_data()`, which report how many observations each filter drops; setting `quiet = FALSE` (the default) is useful when iterating to track sample-construction effects.

For comparison, we also include a bivariate-dependent sort that uses the default filters and breakpoint conventions, so the only difference from the baseline is the addition of size control. The long-short returns from that specification are appended to the customized one in @tbl-customized-comparison.

```{r}
#| label: bivariate-only-sort
options_bivariate <- portfolio_sort_options(
  breakpoint_options_main = breakpoint_options(
    n_portfolios = 5,
    breakpoints_exchanges = "NYSE"
  ),
  breakpoint_options_secondary = breakpoint_options(
    n_portfolios = 2,
    breakpoints_exchanges = "NYSE"
  )
)
portfolio_returns_bivariate <- implement_portfolio_sort(
  data = sorting_data,
  sorting_variables = c("asset_growth", "mktcap_lag"),
  sorting_method = "bivariate-dependent",
  rebalancing_month = 7,
  portfolio_sort_options = options_bivariate
)
factor_returns_bivariate <- portfolio_returns_bivariate |>
  compute_long_short_returns(direction = "bottom_minus_top")
```

@tbl-customized-comparison decomposes the customized premium into two layers. Adding the size-controlled double sort alone (the bivariate-only row) lifts the annualized premium from `{r} round(mean(factor_returns_ag$ret_excess_vw, na.rm = TRUE) * 12 * 100, 1)`% to `{r} round(mean(factor_returns_bivariate$ret_excess_vw, na.rm = TRUE) * 12 * 100, 1)`%, with the $t$~statistic moving from borderline to significant at conventional levels. Controlling for size therefore reveals that most of the AG signal in the cross-section was masked by size dispersion in the univariate sort. Layering the filter set and the 20% breakpoint threshold on top trims the magnitude back to `{r} round(mean(factor_returns_customized$ret_excess_vw, na.rm = TRUE) * 12 * 100, 1)`%, where the spread remains significant at conventional levels: removing financials, utilities, and loss-making firms strips out some of the firms contributing to the unfiltered spread. Across all three specifications, the spread is positive and reflects the negative AG premium reported in @cooper.2008, who finds an annual value-weighted long-short premium of about 12.6% over July 1968 to June 2003.[^cooper-deciles]

[^cooper-deciles]: @cooper.2008 sorts into deciles and reports raw rather than excess returns.

```{r}
#| label: customized-comparison-stats
#| echo: false
customized_comparison_table <- bind_rows(
  factor_returns_ag |>
    drop_na() |>
    summarize(
      Specification = "Baseline (univariate, no filters)",
      `VW mean` = mean(ret_excess_vw) * 12,
      `VW $t$~statistic` = mean(ret_excess_vw) / (sd(ret_excess_vw) / sqrt(n()))
    ),
  factor_returns_bivariate |>
    drop_na() |>
    summarize(
      Specification = "Bivariate only (size-controlled, no filters)",
      `VW mean` = mean(ret_excess_vw) * 12,
      `VW $t$~statistic` = mean(ret_excess_vw) / (sd(ret_excess_vw) / sqrt(n()))
    ),
  factor_returns_customized |>
    drop_na() |>
    summarize(
      Specification = "Customized (size-controlled, filtered)",
      `VW mean` = mean(ret_excess_vw) * 12,
      `VW $t$~statistic` = mean(ret_excess_vw) / (sd(ret_excess_vw) / sqrt(n()))
    )
)
```

```{=latex}
\begingroup
\small
```

```{r}
#| label: tbl-customized-comparison
#| tbl-cap: !expr 'paste0("Comparison of long-short asset growth returns across three specifications. The baseline is a univariate sort with NYSE breakpoints and no filters. The bivariate-only specification adds a dependent double sort on size to the baseline but otherwise keeps the same universe and breakpoints. The customized specification adds the filter set (financials, utilities, non-positive earnings) and a 20\\% size threshold on the breakpoints. All rows use annual July rebalancing; means are annualized value-weighted excess returns. Sample: ", year(date_start), "--", year(date_end), ".")'
#| echo: false
customized_comparison_table |>
  knitr::kable(
    digits = 3,
    escape = FALSE,
```
